invest.model: (a) Any number whose first and last digits match, such as 101, 454, 777. (b) 10 numbers: 202, 212, 222, 232, 242, 252, 262, 272, 282, 292. The first and last digits must both be 2, and the middle digit can be 0 to 9: 10 choices. A child who lists them by the middle digit in order has not missed any. (c) No: 202 is even. A mirror number is even when its first (and last) digit is even. Extension: there are 90 mirror numbers from 100 to 999 (9 choices for the end digits x 10 for the middle). Look for: the child sees that the end digits match, lists in order, and can say why the list is complete.

(a) Ali is right: odd + odd is always even (brute-forced for every pair of 3-digit numbers). (b) Odd + even is always odd; even + even is always even. (c) Taking away behaves the same way: odd − odd is even, odd − even is odd. Why: an odd number is some pairs plus 1 left over, an even number is only pairs. Two odd numbers have two left-overs, and they make one more pair, so no one is left over. Look for: several tests before a claim, then a reason that uses pairs, counters or ones digits, not only “it worked every time”. A ones-digit reason (odd ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9) is also fine.

(a) 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: they jump by 10 and are the 10 times table. (b) 3 and 5: 15, 30, 45 (jump by 15). 4 and 5: 20, 40 (jump by 20). (c) Yes to both, brute-forced up to 100: a number in the 10 table is 10 x something = 2 x (5 x something) = 5 x (2 x something). Child-level reason: a number in the 2 table is even and a number in the 5 table ends in 0 or 5, so a number in both ends in 0, which is the 10 table; and every number in the 10 table ends in 0, so it is even and in the 5 table. Look for: organised lists (writing both tables out and circling), the noticing that the jumps are 10, 15, 20, and a test of “always”.

(a) A: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28. B: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29. C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. (b) Every number is in exactly ONE pattern (brute-forced for 1 to 99). (c) Counting in 3s, a number is either on the 3s (pattern C), 1 more than a number on the 3s (A), or 2 more (B); there is no other choice. (d) 4 patterns, starting at 1, 2, 3 and 4. Look for: a complete listing, the claim “exactly one” tested on more than one number, and a reason that uses the 3 times table.

(a) The final answer is always the number you started with (brute-forced for 1 to 999). (b) Adding 5 then doubling adds 10 and doubles the start; taking away 10 and halving undoes both: (n + 5) x 2 − 10 = n x 2, and half of that is n. A child reason: “double and halve undo each other, and add 5 doubled is 10, which I take away”. (c) Any valid trick, for example: add 3, double, take away 6, halve; or times 4, add 8, divide by 4, take away 2. Check by testing three numbers. Look for: testing small and big numbers, a reason in words, and a trick that really works.

Fewest coins (5¢ to 95¢): 5:1, 10:1, 15:2, 20:1, 25:2, 30:2, 35:3, 40:2, 45:3, 50:1, 55:2, 60:2, 65:3, 70:2, 75:3, 80:3, 85:4, 90:3, 95:4 (brute-forced). (a) 35¢ = 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢, 3 coins. (c) 85¢ and 95¢ need 4 coins each: 85¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ and 95¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 20¢ + 5¢. An amount ending in 5 needs a 5¢ coin, and the rest then needs 3 more coins. Look for: a systematic table, trying biggest coin first, and checking that no smaller number of coins works.

(a) Half: 2 quarters, 3 sixths or 4 eighths (not thirds). (b) Third: 2 sixths only. Quarter: 2 eighths only (checked with exact fractions). (c) No: one third is shorter than a half but two thirds is longer, so no number of thirds fits exactly. Look for: children lay the strips side by side and say “fits exactly”. Keep to the strips and drawings: do not teach “equivalent fractions” as a rule (that is P3).

(a) 2 shapes: a straight line and an L. (b) 5 shapes: a straight line of 4, a 2 x 2 square, an L, a T and a zigzag (S shape). Brute-forced: 1, 1, 2, 5 shapes for 1, 2, 3, 4 squares (turns and flips count as the same). If a child counts flips as different, they find 7 (L and its mirror, S and its mirror): praise this and explain the rule. (c) Look for a system: start with the straight line, then move one square, and check each new shape against the others by turning the tile.

(a) All of them: 1, 2, 1+2 = 3, 4, 1+4 = 5, 2+4 = 6, 1+2+4 = 7. (b) Exactly 2 sets work: 1, 2, 3 (makes 1 to 6) and 1, 2, 4 (makes 1 to 7); brute-forced over all 10 sets. (c) Both contain 1 g and 2 g: only a 1 g weight can make 1 g, and with different weights only a 2 g weight can make 2 g. Look for: a systematic list of the possible sets, checking each mass in order, and the noticing that 1 g is needed.

Number of ways: 1 step: 1, 2 steps: 2, 3 steps: 3, 4 steps: 5, 5 steps: 8 (brute-forced; 6 steps: 13). 4 steps: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2. Pattern: each number is the sum of the two before it (3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13). Look for: a list in order (all 1s first, then swap in a 2), a table, and the pattern spotted from the table. Do not name Fibonacci numbers unless a child asks.
